summary: For ages 5–7, anchor the concept 'rainforest' on three memorable features — HOT, WET (rains almost every day), and near the EQUATOR (the warm middle of the Earth) — and the result: more kinds of plants and animals thrive there than almost anywhere on land. Contrast with a familiar local wood so children feel the difference (warmer, far wetter, green all year, far more life). Seed 'habitat' gently as 'a home that gives living things what they need'. The key insight is the combination: hot + wet + near the Equator makes the crowded green world, which also separates a rainforest from a hot, dry desert.
misconceptions: A rainforest is just any big wood — it is specifically hot, extremely wet, and near the Equator
Rainforests are cold and dark like a spooky forest — they are warm and humid
It rains only sometimes — in a tropical rainforest it rains almost every day
Rainforests are empty and quiet — they hold more kinds of plants and animals than almost anywhere on land
Rainforests are found all over, including cold places — tropical rainforests cluster near the warm Equator

activities.title: Explore a rainforest scene and find its three features
steps: Look closely at a lush rainforest picture full of parrots, monkeys, frogs and vines; describe what you see, and imagine what you would hear and feel if you were there (dripping leaves, warm damp air, animal noise).

Find and name the rain cloud, the thermometer, and the Equator on a small globe; say what each one tells you: it rains almost every day, it is always hot, and rainforests sit in a green belt around the warm middle of the Earth.
Say in your own words why so many plants and animals can live here.
Put the three features together: hot + lots of rain + near the Equator = a rainforest.
activities.insight: A rainforest is defined by three features working together (hot, very wet, near the Equator), and that combination is why it is the busiest habitat on land — not just any big wood.

activities.title: Compare a rainforest with the woods near you
steps: Look at a local wood and a rainforest side by side.
List how they are different: which is warmer, which is wetter, which stays green all year, which has more kinds of plants and animals.
Use a lift-the-flap or fold-over card to answer 'How is this different from the woods near you?' and stack up: warmer, wetter, green all year, far more life.
Say one sentence that explains what makes a rainforest special compared to an ordinary wood.
activities.insight: A rainforest is not just any big woodland — compared with a typical cooler local wood, it is hotter, far wetter all year, green all year, and packed with far more kinds of life.

activities.title: Rainforest or desert? — telling hot-and-wet from hot-and-dry
steps: Discuss: a hot desert is hot and a rainforest is hot — so why isn't a rainforest just a hot, dry place like a hot desert?
Name the one thing that makes the difference: WATER/rain. A rainforest is hot AND very wet; a hot desert is hot but dry.
Explain how you know: the near-daily rain, together with the year-round warmth, is why rainforest plants grow tall and thick and so many animals live there.

Wonder together about the probing questions (there is no single right answer — give your reasons): Why do the plants grow so tall and thick? Where on a globe would you look — top, bottom, or middle? What might happen if it stopped raining for a whole year?
activities.insight: It is the combination of heat AND lots of rain, near the Equator, that makes a rainforest lush — heat alone (as in a desert) does not.

checkQuestion: A desert is hot and a rainforest is hot — so why isn't a rainforest just a hot, sandy place like a desert? What makes a rainforest different, and how do you know?
checkAnswer: A rainforest is hot AND very wet — it rains almost every day, so it's warm and damp, and that's why so many tall thick plants and lots of animals can live there. A desert is hot but dry. It's the combination of heat and lots of rain, near the Equator, that makes a rainforest.
